newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Nervous wait for Argentine wheat storm report.
newsitem.headline: Nervous wait for Argentine wheat storm report.

text.p: Argentine grain traders faced a nervous weekend Friday awaiting an official assessment of storm damage in key zones of the nation's wheat belt.
Fierce winds, torrential rain and in some places hail have in recent days lashed what was heading to be a bumper crop in parts of southern Buenos Aires province and La Pampa.
Exporters minimized the damage, but the country's main farm lobby said many farmers would suffer losses in both quantity and quality.

Patricio Lamarca, advisor to the government's Agricultural Secretariat, said that no official estimate of the damage would be ready until Monday, after crop inspectors have finished wading through the muddy fields.
One trader agreed it was still hard to say how much damage had been done, but he added, "But whatever happens, there's going to be a lot of wheat which has been washed out."
This will mean that the wheat has a lower protein level and is less suitable for making wheat.

A crop analyst who asked not to be identified said he had heard reports of about 100,000 hectares of wheat seriously affected, out of a total sown area of around seven million hectares. He said that some fields were lashed by gale force winds in severe storms.

"That can make it very difficult to get at it with the combines. If it's flattened by winds it's very difficult to harvest, so the quality damage will come from both wetness and if it lies on the ground more moisture will seep into the wheat and damage it," the analyst said.

An exporter said he was not so worried about the reports, and that at most 100,000 tonnes or 200,000 tonnes could have been lost. He was still predicting a crop between 15.5 million tonnes and 16 million tonnes.
The exporter added that if some wheat loses quality it will probably be mixed with better wheat from other areas.
But a farmer from near Necochea in southern Buenos Aires, the heart of Argentina's wheat belt, told Reuters he thought damage had been widespread and serious.

"The weather really hit southwest Buenos Aires and bits of La Pampa hard," he said, speaking by telephone from his farm. "There is barley that is completely lost and the wheat is sprouting in the ear, so the quality becomes feedwheat quality. You can't export it."
"There were places which had 12 inches of rain in one day," he said.

Rural Society spokesman Carlos Dowdall said while it was clear many producers had been hard hit, it was still too early to estimate damage to overall production. He said there was damage in southwest Buenos Aires, La Pampa and south Cordoba.
Recently sown maize and sunflower have also been hit, he said, but not as seriously as the wheat. "There's still time for maize and sunflower to recover."
Up till now, goodish weather had led market players to steadily raise their forecasts for wheat output, which will be up from about 9.2 million tonnes in drought-blighted 1995/96.
The government expects exports to more than double to around 10 million tonnes and said Monday that commitments to foreign buyers had already reached 5.7 million tonnes.

Argentina's Meteorological Service predicted more isolated storms in southern Buenos Aires Friday, although it forecast temperatures would rise. It said there could also be rain early in the day in La Pampa.
